1.b3 e5 2.Bb2.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal against e5, which has no defender yet, so Black has to spend a move holding it. White lets Black build a broad centre and plans to undermine it later with the flank pawns and the other bishop, a patient set-up that tests whether the centre can be kept.

1.b3 e5 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop's diagonal and keeps White's development flexible. It is the patient move of the Larsen set-up and usually transposes into the main line. The cost is that e5 is not yet attacked, so Black can choose a set-up first.

1.b3 e5 2.Nf3.strategy: Attacks e5 and develops, but 2...e4 drives the knight away, and after 3.Nd4 c5 it has to leave the centre again while Black gains space. Sound, but it gives Black the easier choice.

1.b3 e5 2.c4.strategy: Reaches an English structure by transposition, with the bishop to come to b2 against e5. Black holds e5 easily and develops, so the bishop gains little at first. Sound, but slower than the main moves.

1.b3 e5 2.d3.strategy: Supports a later e4 and frees d2 for the b1-knight in a quiet set-up with a kingside fianchetto. It challenges neither e5 nor d5, so Black can build a pawn centre unopposed. Sound, but passive.

1.b3 e5 2.d4.strategy: Challenges e5 at once. After 2...exd4 only the queen can recapture, and 3.Qxd4 Nc6 drives it away with a gain of time for Black, while after 2...e4 the d4-pawn blocks the long diagonal that b3 opened for the bishop. Playable, but White gets nothing more than with the main moves.

1.b3 e5 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre at once and lets the bishop and knight work against e5. But Black develops with tempo, since the e4-pawn needs protection, and White gives up the flexibility of the Larsen set-up. Sound, but it promises no more than Bb2.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops a knight and covers e4 and d5. The knight blocks the c-pawn and the long diagonal of a bishop on b2, and it does not stop Black from taking the centre. Playable, but the knight commits before White's plan is clear.

1.b3 e5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2 for a double fianchetto, with bishops on b2 and g2 aiming at the long diagonals. It leaves the centre to Black, and e5 is not attacked until the bishop reaches b2. Sound, but not testing.

1.b3 e5 2.a3.strategy: Stops ...Bb4 but develops nothing and does not touch the centre. The a3-pawn has no further task, so White is a tempo behind.

1.b3 e5 2.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space and covers b5, but takes no part in the fight for the centre. Black develops freely while White's pawn has no further task.

1.b3 e5 2.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 to build a broad centre, but the pawn blocks the long diagonal that b3 was meant to open for the bishop. Black gets to the centre first, and White needs further tempi to catch up.

1.b3 e5 2.f3.strategy: Supports a later e4, but takes f3, the g1-knight's best square, and weakens the e1-h4 diagonal, so that 2...Qh4+ forces 3.g3. White trades development for a slow structure.

1.b3 e5 2.Nh3.strategy: Heads for f4 or g5, but the e5-pawn already covers f4 and the knight stands on the rim. After 2...d5 the c8-bishop eyes h3, and ...Bxh3 gxh3 doubles White's h-pawns.

1.b3 e5 2.Na3.strategy: Aims at c4, from where the knight would hit e5, but leaves it on the rim, away from the centre. Black takes the centre with ...d5, which also covers c4, while the knight still has to find a useful square.

1.b3 e5 2.Ba3.strategy: Offers to trade the bishop that b3 was meant to bring to the long diagonal, and after 2...Bxa3 3.Nxa3 the recapturing knight stands on the rim. White loses time and Black takes the centre.

1.b3 e5 2.h3.strategy: A waiting move that prevents ...Bg4 but neither develops a piece nor contests the centre. Black builds the centre while the bishop on c1 is still to be developed.

1.b3 e5 2.h4.strategy: Aims for h5 and space on the kingside but takes no part in the centre and leaves g4 uncovered. Black develops freely and takes space in the centre.

1.b3 e5 2.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn with no development behind it: 2...Bxb4 wins it, and the pressure on e5 that follows is easily met, leaving White a pawn down for nothing.

1.b3 e5 2.f4.strategy: Offers the f-pawn without a lead in development: 2...exf4 wins it, and the weakened e1-h4 diagonal makes ...Qh4+ a constant threat. White has no compensation for the pawn.

1.b3 e5 2.g4.strategy: Gains kingside space but leaves the pawn without support: ...d5 opens the c8-bishop against g4, and f3 and h3 are weakened for good while nothing is developed.

1.b3 e5.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack: Modern Variation
1.b3 e5.background: Black's most popular and ambitious reply to 1.b3, chosen in about 45 percent of games.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5.strategy: Puts a second pawn in the centre at once. White's a3 does nothing against the pair on e5 and d5, so Black stands more comfortably in the middle and White can only fight it from the wings. Black has the simplest game: develop and let White find a plan.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 Nc6.strategy: Defends e5 and develops in one move, the natural way to hold the centre pawn. Black keeps the choice of a second central pawn for later and is simply a useful tempo ahead, since White's a3 has done little for the fight for the centre.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and watches e4 and d5, but leaves e5 without a defender: once the bishop reaches b2 it attacks the pawn, so Black must then spend a move on support. The pawn is not lost, but the move gives White something to aim at.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3.strategy: Builds a pawn wall but blocks its own bishop: with pawns on b3 and c3, a queen's bishop on b2 would look at its own pawn, the very fianchetto the b3 pawn was meant for. Three queenside pawn moves and none that contests the centre leave White well behind.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.Bb2.strategy: Puts the bishop on its long diagonal at once, where it attacks the e5 pawn. Black has not protected it yet, so Black must spend a move on it, and White gets the set-up the b3 pawn was played for. The a3 pawn already keeps a black bishop off b4.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.e3.strategy: A patient move that frees the king's bishop and leaves b2 available for the queen's bishop. White lets Black keep the pawn centre for now and plans to undermine it later; the price is a little time, since e5 is not yet under pressure.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c4.strategy: Strikes at d5 before the pawn is established, but the cost is real. If Black pushes the d-pawn, it gains space and blocks the long diagonal White's bishop wants; if Black takes on c4, the recapture leaves White's queenside pawns scattered on a3 and c4.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a purpose: the knight eyes e4 and supports d5, so a central push by White would be hard to carry out. Black needs nothing special; development and castling are enough against a set-up that does not challenge the centre.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nc6.strategy: Guards e5 with a developing move and adds control of d4, so White cannot easily build a centre. Black's pawns stay supported and the knight keeps the other pieces free to develop.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 e4.strategy: Gains space and takes d3 and f3 away from White's pieces. The pawn is then fixed on e4, where White can attack it, and it needs the d5 pawn behind it; Black cramps White, but commits the centre before developing a piece.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Controls e4 and prepares to meet the centre with a pawn of its own, but it is slow and blocks the king's bishop's route to the queenside. White's pawns form a wall on the third rank with the pieces behind, a solid but passive set-up from which Black can develop at leisure.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Challenges the centre at once: e5 is unprotected, so Black must push past the pawn, exchange it or defend it. White's c3 and d4 pawns form a solid core, and the bishop on c1 gets its diagonal open. White fights for the centre instead of waiting behind a wall of pawns.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.e3.strategy: A solid, patient move that frees the king's bishop and prepares to meet Black's centre later. It shuts in the queen's bishop, and Black is left free to develop and take more space, so White must reply accurately.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 at once, but White has already used three pawn moves on the queenside and now loosens the structure there further. After the exchange on c4 the pawns are scattered, and if Black pushes instead, the centre closes in Black's favour.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the second knight, defends e5 and eyes d4, so White cannot easily establish a pawn there. Black's centre is fully supported and the game is Black's to steer, with White still looking for a way to challenge it.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 Bd6.strategy: Defends the e5 pawn from behind and prepares to castle, while the bishop eyes the a3 pawn that White's pieces guard. It asks little of White's set-up, a little passive, but it keeps Black's centre fully supported.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 e4.strategy: Pushes forward to cramp White: the pawn attacks d3 and takes f3 away from the king's knight. White can exchange on e4 at once, and Black must then recapture with the knight, because taking back with the d-pawn allows a queen trade that costs Black the right to castle.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 Nc6 5.e3.strategy: Covers d4 against the knight and keeps a push to e4 in reserve as the way to challenge Black's centre. But it locks the queen's bishop in, leaving it only b2 and d2. White builds a compact wall at the cost of piece play.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 Nc6 5.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight puts pressure on e5, which Black must keep protected, and clears the way to castle. It does not yet challenge Black's centre, but it is the sound development White needs before looking for a break.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 Nc6 5.Bg5.strategy: Brings the queen's bishop out on an open diagonal, outside the pawn chain, and increases the pressure on f6, so the knight that supports the centre is harassed. The bishop is active instead of being left boxed in behind its own pawns.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 Nc6 5.e3 B.strategy: A solid developing move: the bishop backs up the e5 pawn from behind, clears the way to castle and eyes the a3 pawn, though that is guarded. Black keeps every pawn defended and loses nothing in the centre while White's pieces remain boxed in.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 Nc6 5.e3 e.strategy: Gains space and attacks the d3 pawn, taking f3 away from White's king's knight. The pawn fixes the centre in Black's favour and keeps White's pieces cramped, but it can become a target if Black neglects its support.

1.b3 e5 2.a3 d5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3 Nc6 5.e3 B.strategy: Brings the bishop out quietly and prepares to castle, but from e7 it does not support the e5 pawn, which then rests on the knight alone. Safe and sound, if a little passive.

Backs a later e4, but takes f3 from the king's knight, which is left with only e2 and h3, and does nothing about Black's lead in the centre. A slow, cramped way to finish the pawn wall when development still comes first.

Brings the king's knight to its natural square, which the f-pawn leaves free, where it presses on e5 and prepares to castle. White gets a compact, flexible position. It is still short of a central plan, but nothing is wrong with it.

Develops the king's bishop towards castling and keeps the knight's best square free. It is solid and it leaves the structure alone, but the bishop aims at no target and White still has to find a way to challenge Black's centre.

Adds control of e4 to prepare a central break, but the knight takes its own bishop's best exit, leaving the bishop on c1 only the b2 square. A slow, cramped way to develop that still does not hurry the break.

Castles, putting the king to safety and bringing the rook towards the centre before anything happens. White's pawn wall has no active plan yet, so Black can castle first and pick the right moment for a central break.

Strikes at the pawns f3 has left: the pawn attacks d3 and f3, and an exchange on e4 loosens White's king's side, since the f-pawn disappears and the king's diagonal opens. Black gets active play against a self-weakened structure.

Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, where it eyes d3 and keeps watch on e4, so White's central break is harder to carry out. A sound move, but the bishop can be harassed later and Black does not yet castle.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack: Modern Variation
1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6.background: The more common of the two natural ways to defend the e5-pawn after 2.Bb2; the other is 2...d6. A model game is Bent Larsen against Brian Eley, Hastings 1972, won by White after 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bb5 d6 5.Ne2.
1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6.strategy: The natural defence: the knight guards e5 and develops in one move, and Black stays free to take the centre with the d-pawn too. The cost is the c-pawn, which can no longer support the centre from c6. White usually lets Black build a broad centre and attacks it later from the flanks, a patient fight over who controls the centre in the end.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 d6.strategy: A modest defence: the pawn holds e5, keeps the structure compact and frees the c8-bishop, but it takes d6 from the f8-bishop, which is left with e7. Black gives up the chance of a broad pawn centre in return for solidity. The game stays quiet, with Black a little cramped but solid and White free to build up slowly.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Qe7.strategy: Defends e5, but the queen blocks the f8-bishop and invites a knight to attack it with tempo. Sound enough, yet a knight or a pawn is the more natural defender, and the f8-bishop stays shut in.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Bd6.strategy: Defends e5 with the bishop, but it stands in front of the d-pawn, so neither ...d6 nor ...d5 is possible and the c8-bishop stays shut in until the bishop moves again. A white knight gains time against it. Playable, but less harmonious than a knight or pawn defending e5.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nf6.strategy: Develops but leaves e5 en prise: 3.Bxe5 Nc6 4.Bb2 wins a clean pawn. Black's lead in development is only modest compensation.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 d5.strategy: Strikes in the centre but ignores the attack on e5: 3.Bxe5 wins a clean pawn. Black's lead in development is not enough to pay for it.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Qf6.strategy: Defends e5, but takes the natural f6 square from the g8-knight and exposes the queen. A white knight gains time against it, and once the e5-pawn leaves, the b2-bishop hits f6 too.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 f6.strategy: Holds e5 with a pawn, but takes f6 from the g8-knight and loosens the e8–h5 diagonal, so the knight must develop on e7 or h6. Sound but clumsy, and White develops freely.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 e4.strategy: Gains space and moves the pawn out of the bishop's sight, but it stands unsupported on e4 and White can attack it with development or undermine it with a pawn. Sound, yet Black must keep spending time on it.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim and does nothing about the attack on e5: 3.Bxe5 wins a clean pawn, and the knight on a6 is far from the centre and the kingside.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nh6.strategy: Sends the knight to the rim, where it guards f7 but not e5: 3.Bxe5 wins a pawn for free.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Ne7.strategy: Blocks the f8-bishop and does not defend e5: 3.Bxe5 wins a pawn. Black can gain some time by chasing the bishop with the knight, but the pawn does not come back.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Qg5.strategy: Defends e5 along the rank and eyes g2, which Bf1 covers. 3.Nf3 attacks queen and e5 together, and once the queen moves, e5 is attacked twice and falls.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Qh4.strategy: Eyes f2 and h2 but leaves e5 undefended. 3.Bxe5 wins a pawn at once, and 3.Nf3 attacks queen and e5 together, so the early queen only loses time.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Ke7.strategy: Blocks the queen and the f8-bishop, gives up castling and leaves e5 hanging: 3.Bxe5 wins a pawn for nothing, and the king stays in the centre.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop but leaves e5 hanging, and with the f8-bishop gone g7 is loose: 3.Bxe5 wins the pawn and threatens Bxg7 and the h8-rook. Black parries with a developing move, but remains a pawn down.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Bc5.strategy: Eyes f2 but leaves e5 hanging. 3.Bxe5 wins the pawn and also threatens Bxg7 and the h8-rook, since the f8-bishop no longer guards g7.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Bb4.strategy: Develops with an eye on c3 but leaves e5 hanging, and without the f8-bishop g7 is loose: 3.Bxe5 wins the pawn and threatens Bxg7. White can also gain a tempo against the bishop later.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Ba3.strategy: Walks into Nxa3 or Bxa3: the bishop is attacked twice and not defended, so it simply loses a piece for nothing.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook pawn and ignores the attack on e5: 3.Bxe5 wins a pawn for nothing.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 a5.strategy: Advances a rook pawn without defending e5, so 3.Bxe5 wins a pawn; the pawn on a5 also weakens the b5 square.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, but 3.Bxe5 takes the e-pawn first and ...Bb7 cannot win it back.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 b5.strategy: Gains queenside space and prepares ...Bb7, but ignores e5: 3.Bxe5 wins the pawn, and the advanced b-pawn gives White further targets.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 but leaves e5 hanging: 3.Bxe5 wins the pawn, and ...c6 also takes the natural c6 square from the b8-knight.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 c5.strategy: Takes space on the queenside but ignores the attack on e5: 3.Bxe5 Nc6 4.Bb2 leaves White a pawn up for only a little queenside space.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 f5.strategy: Takes e4 away in Dutch style but does not defend e5: 3.Bxe5 wins a pawn, and the e8–h5 diagonal is weakened.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto, but once e5 falls the long diagonal reaches the h8-rook: 3.Bxe5 wins the pawn with an attack on h8, so Black must spend the next move defending the rook.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 g5.strategy: Opens the long diagonal to h8 and ignores e5: 3.Bxe5 wins the pawn and attacks the h8-rook, so Black must answer the attack and has weakened the kingside for nothing.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 h6.strategy: Wastes a tempo on a rook pawn and ignores the attack on e5: 3.Bxe5 wins a pawn.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 h5.strategy: Gains kingside space without defending e5: 3.Bxe5 wins the pawn, and the pawn on h5 weakens g5 and g6.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6 3.e3.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack: Modern Variation
1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6 3.e3.strategy: The typical plan: White lets Black have pawns on e5 and d5 and prepares to undermine them later. The move opens the king's bishop, which can pressure the knight guarding e5. The game becomes a patient fight of White's flank pieces against a big black centre.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6 3.c4.strategy: Stops Black from setting up a pawn on d5 for free by fighting for that square with a flank pawn. White leaves the centre to Black, so the play is slow and manoeuvring.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6 3.f4.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack: Pachman Gambit
1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6 3.f4.strategy: Hits e5 twice at once, with pawn and bishop against one defender, and offers the f-pawn to open the position. But Black simply takes it, winning a pawn, and the move opens the e1-h4 diagonal to a check on h4. The long diagonal and e-file are thin compensation.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6 3.c4 Nf6.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack: Modern Variation
1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6 3.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the second knight and adds pressure on e4 and d5, the squares White would need for a central break. Black gets a sound, flexible position: e5 is guarded and White's early pawn move has not stopped Black from challenging the centre on good terms.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6 3.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop for a slow, closed game, while Nc6 still protects e5. Black keeps the centre intact and waits to see where White commits; the plan is solid and flexible, but less direct than developing the knight.

1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6 3.c4 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and opens the bishop on c8, a safe and modest set-up. It blocks the king's bishop's diagonal and gives White an easy game, since Black has not yet challenged the centre.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight and defends e5 against the coming Bb2 without committing a pawn, so Black can still choose a broad centre or a more flexible set-up. The cost is that the knight blocks the c-pawn, so ...c5 is not available for now.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once: Black has pawns on d5 and e5 before White has developed a piece. The d-pawn does not defend e5, so Bb2 still has to be met, and the broad centre needs support to avoid becoming a target. In return Black gains space and sets the agenda early.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Nf6.strategy: Develops toward the centre and watches e4 and d5, keeping Black's pawn moves flexible. The knight does not defend e5, so Black needs another move to meet Bb2, which comes with gain of time.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal, a solid, compact set-up. The cost is some passivity, since a pawn on d6 claims less central space than one on d5, so Black plays for security rather than for space.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Be7.strategy: Prepares castling and keeps the pawns flexible, but the bishop neither defends e5 nor contests the centre. 3.Bb2 attacks e5 at once, so Black spends the next move holding it.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Bd6.strategy: Defends e5 and prepares castling, but the bishop blocks the d7-pawn, so neither ...d6 nor ...d5 is possible until it moves again. The c8-bishop stays shut in as well unless Black spends a move on ...b6.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, a fianchetto mirroring White's, with the bishop aimed at g2. e5 is still undefended, so 3.Bb2 forces a defence first, since 3...Bb7 drops the pawn to 4.Bxe5.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with the c6-pawn behind it and keeps White's bishop and knight off b5. It develops nothing, though, and 3.Bb2 forces Black to spend a move holding e5.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 c5.strategy: Takes space on the queenside and prepares to develop with support for e5, but with pawns on c5 and e5 no black pawn can guard d5 any more, a hole for a white knight after c4 and Nc3. e5 also still needs a defender against 3.Bb2.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7, which defends e5 along the long diagonal, so 3.Bb2 can be met by 3...Bg7. The set-up is sound but slow, and the e5-pawn then blocks the bishop's diagonal, so the bishop defends rather than attacks.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Na6.strategy: A rim knight that eyes b4 and c5 but does not defend e5, so 3.Bb2 costs Black another move to hold the pawn. 3.Bxa6 bxa6 also doubles Black's a-pawns.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Qe7.strategy: Defends e5 but shuts in the f8-bishop, whose only open diagonal runs through e7. 3.Ba3 attacks the queen at once, so Black must block or move it. Sound, but White gains time while the bishop stays shut in.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Qf6.strategy: Brings the queen out early and takes f6 from the king's knight. It defends e5, but 3.Nc3 threatens Nd5, hitting the queen and c7, and Ne4 can also gain time against it.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Qg5.strategy: The queen eyes g2, which the f1-bishop guards, so nothing is threatened. 3.Nf3 attacks queen and e5 at once, and after a retreat to e7 or f6 White has developed with tempo.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Qh4.strategy: The queen attacks nothing, since f2 and h2 are both guarded. 3.Nf3 hits queen and e5 together, and the queen needs a second move to reach e7 or f6, squares it could have reached at once.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Bc5.strategy: The e3-pawn blunts the bishop on the a7–g1 diagonal, and 3.d4 hits bishop and e5 at once, so White gains time and space in the centre.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Bb4.strategy: Develops the bishop, but its only target is the d2-pawn, which has four defenders, and 3.a3 sends it away again. It also leaves e5 undefended against Bb2. Sound, though White gains time.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Nh6.strategy: A rim knight that covers f5 and g4 but not the centre, and it leaves e5 without a defender, which 3.Bb2 attacks at once. Unlike ...Nf6, it has no say over d5 or e4.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Ne7.strategy: Blocks the f8-bishop and the queen and does not defend e5, which 3.Bb2 attacks at once. The knight can reach c6 or g6 later, but only at the cost of another move.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 a6.strategy: Prevents Bb5 and prepares ...b5, but develops nothing, and e5 still needs a defender against Bb2. Harmless, yet slow.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space and prepares ...a4 against the b3-pawn, but develops nothing, and e5 still needs a defender against Bb2. Sound, though slow.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 f6.strategy: Defends e5 but takes f6 from the king's knight and opens the e8–h5 diagonal: 3.Qh5+ forces ...g6 or ...Ke7. Black is left with weakened light squares and no development.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 f5.strategy: Takes e4 away from White and grabs space, but opens the e8–h5 diagonal and leaves e5 without a defender against Bb2. Sound, yet the king is loosened and White develops with tempo.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 g5.strategy: Gains space but creates holes on f5 and h5, and 3.h4 undermines the pawn at once. The kingside is weakened for no development in return.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 h6.strategy: Covers g5 but does nothing for development or the centre, and e5 still needs a defender against Bb2. Harmless, yet slow.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 h5.strategy: Starts a flank advance without developing a piece. The pawn on h5 is defended only by the rook, so Be2 with the queen behind it can attack it twice, and e5 still lacks a defender against Bb2. Harmless, but Black loses time.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 e4.strategy: Gains space, but the advanced pawn has no support and 3.d3 challenges it at once; once it is traded, White's bishop is developed. The advance also clears the long diagonal for Bb2 toward g7.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Ke7.strategy: Forfeits castling and blocks the queen and the f8-bishop for no return. 3.Ba3+ checks at once along the a3–f8 diagonal, so Black must block with a pawn, which is then pinned or lost, or lose more time moving the king again.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 Ba3.strategy: Walks into the diagonal of the c1-bishop: 3.Bxa3 or 3.Nxa3 wins the piece for nothing.

1.b3 e5 2.e3 b5.strategy: Hangs the pawn: 3.Bxb5 takes it for free, as nothing defends b5 and Black has no development lead to compensate.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a second pawn and controls e4, the square White's knight and e-pawn want. The pawn also leaves Black the option of gaining space and harassing the knight by pushing again. Black stands comfortably in the middle against a slow set-up.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with pressure on e4 and d5, the squares White's knight and e-pawn want, and Black keeps the choice of centre. It is flexible and sound, though it gives White a move to decide on the set-up before Black declares the pawn structure.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Protects the e5 pawn with a developing move and leaves Black the choice of centre set-ups. It is sound, but asks less of White than taking the centre with a second pawn.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 d5 3.e4.strategy: Strikes at d5 at once: the pawn and the knight both attack it, and only the queen defends it. White opens the centre quickly, before Black's pieces are out, and the bishop that b3 prepares will later bear on the long diagonal.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 d5 3.Bb2.strategy: Completes the plan b3 began, but the bishop looks at nothing: the knight on c3 blocks its diagonal, so it does not even touch e5. Black answers with ...d4, gaining space and a tempo against the knight.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Attacks the e5 pawn, which no black piece defends, and develops a piece. But Black pushes the pawn on with ...e4, attacking the knight, which has to retreat; Black is left with the space in the centre.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 d5 3.e4 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn, but 4.Nxe4 regains it at once, so nothing is won. Material is level and the d-file is open, yet Black has given up the space that ...d4 gains and White's knight lands on a central square. Sound and roughly equal, but second-rate.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 d5 3.e4 d4.strategy: Gains space with a tempo: the pawn drives the knight from c3 and clamps the centre, so White's pieces have fewer good squares. Black accepts a pawn chain that White will try to undermine from the flank, but starts with the better share of the centre.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 d5 3.e4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on the e4 pawn, but White takes on d5 and the knights come off. That clears the long diagonal for the bishop on b2, which then bears down on the e5 pawn and ties Black's queen to its defence.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 d5 3.e4 dxe4 4.d3.name: Dunst Opening: Gladbacher Gambit
1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 d5 3.e4 dxe4 4.d3.strategy: A gambit: White offers a second pawn to drag the e4 pawn away and bring the pieces out with tempo. If Black takes, the bishop recaptures on d3 and aims at the kingside, but White is a pawn down against sound play. Simply regaining the pawn is better.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 d5 3.e4 dxe4 4.Nxe4.strategy: Wins the pawn back at once and puts the knight on a central square. Material is level, the d-file is open, and with the c3 square cleared the bishop on b2 will have the long diagonal for itself. White has lost nothing for the pawn it offered.

1.b3 e5 2.Nc3 d5 3.e4 dxe4 4.Nge2.strategy: Develops and prepares Ng3, but does not retake the pawn at once. Black can keep it with ...f5, and the e2-knight shuts in the f1-bishop. White has to prove compensation for a pawn that 4.Nxe4 would simply have regained, and finds little.
